intro/hello: Welcome back. In the Transformer chapter you built the 2017 block: attention, then an MLP, each wrapped in a residual connection and a layer norm.
intro/same: Every large language model is still that block, stacked dozens of times.
intro/but: But open the code of a model trained in 2024, and almost every part of it has been replaced.
intro/list1: The norm moved, and lost its mean. Positions became rotations.
intro/list2: The MLP grew a gate. Query heads now share their keys and values.
intro/list3: Queries and keys got a norm of their own, the biases are gone, and attention is computed in tiles.
intro/why: None of this changes what attention is. Each change fixes a problem that appeared as models got deeper, read longer texts, and served millions of people.
intro/plan: For each one we ask what problem it solves, what it costs, and which picture makes it obvious.
intro/go: We start where the 2017 block is most fragile: the norm sitting on the residual stream.
prenorm/stream: A residual connection makes each layer add to a running vector instead of replacing it: the residual stream.
prenorm/grad: Its great virtue is the gradient: backprop has a direct route from the loss to every layer, through nothing but plus signs.
prenorm/post: The 2017 block put its layer norm on that route: after every sub-block, the whole stream is normalized. That is post-norm.
prenorm/divide: A norm divides by the stream's spread. If a sub-block adds about as much as is already there, the spread grows by root two, and the norm divides it back down.
prenorm/compound: So an early write shrinks by about root two at every layer above it. Over twenty four layers, that estimate is a factor of four thousand.
prenorm/measure: Measured on a random stack, it is near thirteen hundred. Each bar is how strongly one write reaches the top, and the embedding, on the left, barely registers.
prenorm/pre: Pre-norm moves the norm onto the branch. Only the copy entering the sub-block is normalized; the stream is only ever added to.
prenorm/flat: Now the top of the stack is a plain sum of every write, each with weight one. The highway is clear.
prenorm/history: G P T two made this switch in 2019, and deep stacks train without a long, careful warmup.
prenorm/cost: The cost: nothing shrinks the stream, so it grows with depth, and each layer has a smaller relative say. One final norm goes on top.
rmsnorm/ln: Layer norm does two things to a token's vector. First it subtracts the mean, so the numbers average to zero.
rmsnorm/ln2: Then it divides by their spread, so the spread is one. A learned gain and bias can undo either step.
rmsnorm/rms: R M S norm, from Zhang and Sennrich in 2019, keeps only the second step. It divides by the root mean square: square every entry, average, take the square root.
rmsnorm/gain: Then it multiplies by the gain. No mean, and no bias.
rmsnorm/scale: Scale the input up, and both norms give exactly the same output: dividing by a size cancels any common factor.
rmsnorm/shift: Shift the input, and layer norm does not move, but R M S norm does. That lost invariance is the whole price.
rmsnorm/why: The bet was that the rescaling is what matters: it holds each layer's input at a fixed size, however the weights below it drift.
rmsnorm/cheap: It held. The same quality, one pass over the vector instead of two, and nothing to subtract. llama made it the standard.
rope/order: Attention alone has no sense of order. Shuffle the tokens, and the outputs just shuffle along.
rope/old: The 2017 fix added a position vector to each embedding, once, at the bottom of the stack.
rope/problems: Two problems. Attention mostly cares about relative position, like the word just before me, which an absolute vector leaves the model to work out. And a learned table ends where training ended.
rope/rope: rope, from Su and colleagues in 2021, puts position into the one place attention looks: the dot product of a query and a key.
rope/pairs: Split each query and key into pairs of numbers, and treat each pair as an arrow in a plane.
rope/rotate: At position m, rotate pair i by the angle m times theta i. A rotation turns the arrow without changing its length.
rope/both: The key, at its own position n, is rotated by n times theta i.
rope/shift: Now slide both tokens along the sequence. Both arrows turn, but the angle between them stays fixed, and so does their dot product.
rope/relative: The score depends only on the offset between the two positions, n minus m. Relative position, from an operation on each token alone.
rope/speeds: Each pair has its own speed, from one radian per token for the first pair down to about a ten thousandth for the last.
rope/clock: Like the hands of a clock: fast pairs tell neighbors apart, and slow pairs track distance over thousands of tokens.
rope/cost: No parameters and a few multiplications, and only queries and keys are rotated, never values.
swiglu/old: The 2017 MLP is two matrices with a ray-loo between them. Each hidden unit takes one linear feature and clips it at zero.
swiglu/ramp: On a two dimensional input, one such unit is a ramp: flat on one side of a line, rising steadily on the other.
swiglu/glu: A gated linear unit computes two linear features and multiplies them, one passed through an activation that acts as a gate.
swiglu/silu: swig-loo gates with sigh-loo: z times the sigmoid of z, a smooth ray-loo that dips slightly below zero.
swiglu/product: Now one unit is a product of two directions: near zero along two lines, positive in two regions, negative in the others.
swiglu/why: That lets a unit say: this feature, scaled by that one. Noam Shazeer tried several gates in 2020, and this one made the best language models.
swiglu/size: Three matrices instead of two, so the hidden layer shrinks from four times the model width to eight thirds, keeping the parameter count the same.
swiglu/shrug: Why it works so well is mostly empirical. Shazeer's paper credits divine benevolence.
swiglu/adopt: palm and llama adopted it, and it is now the default.
kvcache/loop: Generating text is a loop: run the model, sample one token, append it, and repeat.
kvcache/same: In a causal model, earlier tokens only look backward, so their keys and values never change when a new token arrives.
kvcache/cache: So a server keeps them. That is the K V cache. Each new token computes only its own query, key and value,
kvcache/store: stores its key and value, and attends over everything stored.
kvcache/mem: That trades compute for memory, and the memory adds up: one key and one value per token, in every layer, for every key-value head.
kvcache/formula: So bytes per token are two, times layers, times key-value heads, times head width, times bytes per number.
kvcache/llama: For llama two, seven B: two, times thirty two layers, times thirty two heads, times a hundred and twenty eight, times two bytes. Half a megabyte, for every token.
kvcache/ctx: Its full context of about four thousand tokens takes two gigabytes per sequence, next to thirteen for the weights.
kvcache/batch: Serve thirty two sequences at once, and the cache is sixty four gigabytes: five times the model itself.
kvcache/speed: And each new token reads the whole cache from memory, so its size sets the speed, not just the capacity.
gqa/mha: Multi-head attention gives every query head its own key and value head: thirty two query heads, thirty two of each.
gqa/mqa: Multi-query attention, from Noam Shazeer in 2019, keeps all the query heads but shares a single key and value head among them.
gqa/mqa2: The cache shrinks thirty two times. But quality drops a little, and training can get less stable.
gqa/gqa: Grouped-query attention, from Ainslie and colleagues in 2023, is the middle ground: groups of query heads, each group sharing one key and value head.
gqa/repeat: In code, each shared key and value head is simply reused by every query head in its group.
gqa/quality: With eight groups it comes close to full multi-head quality, at a quarter of the cache.
gqa/llama3: llama three, eight B is about the size of llama two, seven B, but keeps eight key-value heads: a hundred and twenty eight kilobytes per token, not five hundred and twelve.
gqa/further: deep seek V two went further, caching one small compressed vector per token. Paged caches and batching come later, in fast inference.
stability/growth: An attention score is a query times a key. If training slowly grows the weights that make them, both vectors grow, and the score grows with their product.
stability/collapse: Large scores make the softmax nearly one-hot: one key takes almost all of the attention.
stability/stuck: A saturated softmax passes almost no gradient to the other keys, and training can stall, or diverge.
stability/vit: This derailed a twenty two billion parameter vision transformer in 2023: its attention logits had grown enormous.
stability/fix: The fix is Q K norm: normalize each query and each key, right before the dot product.
stability/bounded: Now every score is bounded, however large the weights grow. Attention can still sharpen, but only on purpose, through the gains.
stability/who: olmo two, gemma three and kwen three all use it.
stability/biases: palm dropped every bias in 2022, and reported more stable training.
stability/keybias: Some biases never did anything. A bias on the keys adds the same number to every score in a row.
stability/cancel: And softmax ignores a constant added to all its inputs, so that bias never changed the output. Its gradient is exactly zero.
flash/two: A GPU has two kinds of memory that matter here. H B M is large, tens of gigabytes, but comparatively slow.
flash/sram: S ram sits on the chip, next to the arithmetic: about ten times faster, but tiny, a couple of hundred kilobytes per unit.
flash/wait: The arithmetic is so fast that many operations spend most of their time waiting on H B M.
flash/standard: Standard attention is one of them. It writes the full T by T matrix of scores out to H B M,
flash/readback: reads it back for the softmax, writes the weights, and reads them again to multiply by the values.
flash/size: At eight thousand tokens, one head's score matrix is a hundred and twenty eight megabytes, for every head, layer and sequence.
flash/tiles: The fix: load a block of queries and a block of keys into S ram, compute that block of scores there, and never write it out.
flash/snag: One thing stands in the way: the softmax needs a row's maximum and its sum, over all the keys, before it can finish any output.
flash/next: Getting around that takes one small trick.
online/idea: The trick, from Milakov and Gimelshein in 2018, is the online softmax. Keep three running numbers for each query.
online/three: The largest score so far, m. A running sum of exponentials, l. And a running output, o, not yet divided by l.
online/tile1: Load the first tile of four keys. Its largest score becomes m, and every exponential is taken relative to it.
online/tile2: The second tile holds a bigger score. So every old term was computed against a maximum that was too small.
online/fix: They are all off by the same factor, so multiplying the old sum and the old output by e to the old max minus the new max corrects them all at once.
online/add: Then add the new tile's terms on top.
online/tile3: The third tile, the same move again. Each tile is touched once, and then it is gone.
online/done: At the end, o divided by l is the softmax-weighted average of the values,
online/same: exactly the number the direct formula gives, up to rounding.
online/flash: FlashAttention, from Tri Dao and colleagues in 2022, runs this loop for blocks of queries and keys inside one kernel. Memory grows linearly with length, and attention got several times faster.
online/exact: It is exact, not an approximation. The backward pass recomputes tiles instead of storing them: more arithmetic, far less memory traffic.
longctx/why: Long training sequences are expensive and most documents are short, so models pretrain at a few thousand tokens and are stretched near the end.
longctx/breaks: Feed a model longer text than it trained on, and it usually falls apart past that length. The clock picture says why.
longctx/wave: Each rope pair turns once every so many tokens: its wavelength. Fast pairs turn many times in the training window, so they have seen every angle.
longctx/slow: But the slowest pairs, with wavelengths in the tens of thousands, never finished a single turn in a four thousand token window.
longctx/unseen: Past that length, they produce angles the model has never seen.
longctx/pi: Position interpolation, from Chen and colleagues in 2023, divides every speed by the stretch factor. Nothing is unseen, but neighbors become harder to tell apart.
longctx/ntk: N T K aware scaling raises the base instead. The fastest pair is untouched, and the slowest slows by exactly the stretch factor.
longctx/yarn: yarn decides pair by pair. Pairs that turned many times keep their speed, pairs that never turned are interpolated, with a blend in between.
longctx/base: Or start with a bigger base: llama three uses five hundred thousand, and llama three point one stretched to a hundred and twenty eight thousand tokens.
longctx/window: Another way to bound the cost is sliding window attention: most layers only look a few thousand tokens back.
outro/r1: So here is the modern block. Pre-norm keeps the residual stream a clean sum, and R M S norm keeps only the rescaling that mattered.
outro/r2: rope rotates queries and keys, so scores depend on relative position.
outro/r3: swig-loo puts a gate in the MLP.
outro/r4: Grouped-query attention shrinks the K V cache: two, times layers, times key-value heads, times head width, times bytes, per token.
outro/r5: Q K norm bounds the scores, and the biases are gone.
outro/r6: FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles, so the score matrix never touches slow memory.
outro/r7: And rescaling rope's speeds stretches a model past the context it trained on.
outro/next: Each change keeps the same block, only cheaper, steadier, or longer reaching. Next: the optimizers that train these blocks at scale.
